chunks: Al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿUbayd Allāh informed me, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, from his father, from Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā al-Ashʿarī, from al-ʿAmrakī, from ʿAlī ibn Jaʿfar, from his brother Mūsā ibn Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said:

I asked him about a man who slaughtered a sheep, and it convulsed and fell into a water well while its veins were gushing blood. May wudu (ablution) be performed from that well? He said: Thirty to forty buckets are drawn from it, then wudu (ablution) is performed, and there is no harm in it.

He said: And I asked him about a man who slaughtered a chicken or a pigeon and it fell into a well. Is it suitable that wudu (ablution) be performed from it? He said: A few buckets are drawn from it, then wudu (ablution) is performed from it.
And I asked him about a man drawing water from a well and having a nosebleed into it. May he perform wudu (ablution) from it? He said: A few buckets are drawn from it.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on performing wudu (ablution) from a well into which blood has fallen?
ai.summary: This hadith gives legal rulings on a well into which blood falls in varying amounts. It states that a specified amount of water should be drawn out before using the well water for wudu (ablution), with a larger amount required when a slaughtered sheep falls into it and a smaller amount for a chicken, pigeon, or nosebleed. Its significance lies in detailing practical rulings of ritual purity in cases of contamination.
